chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the man who is present at the accounting/settlement of a man, and they (both) seek from him testimony about what he heard from them. He said: That is up to him — if he wishes, he testifies, and if he wishes, he does not testify. Then if he testifies, it would be with the truth of what he heard. And if he does not testify, then there is nothing against him, because the two of them did not make him a witness (beforehand).

key_terms.الحساب: Accounting/settlement — financial reckoning or dispute resolution between parties
key_terms.الشهادة: Testimony — a formal legal act in Islamic law with specific requirements
key_terms.بحق: With truth — the condition under which testimony is morally valid
key_terms.يشهدانه: They make him a witness — the formal act of appointing a witness beforehand

ai.seo_question: Is a person who overhears a financial agreement obligated to testify in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) rules that a person who merely happens to be present at a financial settlement between two parties is not obligated to testify, because formal witness status requires being explicitly appointed as such at the time of the transaction. This hadith addresses a recurring situation in early Muslim commercial life, where merchants and property holders would settle accounts in the presence of others. Imam al-Baqir clarifies that voluntary presence does not create a binding duty to testify — a crucial distinction between a formal witness (shahid) deliberately appointed and a casual bystander.
